Ask them to show their work, and the conversation usually ends. That gap — between the number in the schedule and the evidence on the ground — is what construction progress tracking is supposed to close, and on most infrastructure projects it still doesn’t. This guide covers what construction progress tracking actually requires on linear infrastructure work: what to measure, how to capture it, how to turn raw site data into a weighted completion figure, and how to get that figure in front of stakeholders without a week of manual assembly. Along the way, it links out to the deeper how-to guides on each step. What construction progress tracking means in heavy civil work In vertical construction, progress is relatively easy to bound. Floors are discrete. Trades finish and move on. A superintendent can walk a level and form a defensible judgment. Linear infrastructure does not behave that way. A roadway, rail alignment, or utility corridor stretches for kilometers. Work happens simultaneously at stations that are nowhere near each other. Quantities are continuous — cubic meters of embankment, linear meters of barrier, counts of culverts and manholes — and the contract bills in those same units. Nobody can walk it in the morning. So construction progress tracking on heavy civil work has to answer a harder question: of the total contracted quantity, how much is physically in place right now, and what does that imply about the completion date? That requires four things working together: A schedule that defines the activities and their planned dates — usually Primavera P6 or Microsoft Project. A design that defines what “finished” looks like in CAD, IFC, or a full model. Site capture that records what is actually built, at a cadence fast enough to be useful. A method for reconciling the three into a single number that survives scrutiny. Most projects have the first three. Very few have the fourth. Our piece on what Homer can teach heavy civil about progress tracking makes the case that this is not a new problem — it is a very old one about knowing where you actually are versus where you think you are. Why manual progress tracking breaks down The update cycle is slower than the site Site conditions change weekly. Schedules get updated monthly, if that. By the time a percent-complete figure reaches the owner, it describes a project that no longer exists. Every downstream decision—resourcing, sequencing, the pay application—is made using stale data. The number is a judgment, not a measurement Somebody walks the site, forms an impression, and types a figure into the schedule. That figure moves real money. When an owner challenges it, there is rarely an artifact to point to. Our guide to automated construction progress tracking tools goes deeper into why replacing the estimate with a measurement changes the conversation. The data lives in three systems that don’t talk Design sits in CAD or IFC. The schedule sits in P6. Site reality sits in drone flights, photos, and someone’s phone. Reconciling them is manual, slow, and lossy. A connected data environment is the structural fix, and disciplined construction data management is what keeps it from degrading over the life of the job. Nobody can quantify the slip Everyone on a struggling project knows which activities are behind. Almost nobody can say by how many days, or what that does to the forecast completion date. Without weighted, quantity-based measurement, “we’re behind” is a feeling rather than a forecast. The cost of all this is not abstract. September 1, 2026 Introducing DatuBIM Progress Tracking: Percent Complete You Can Defend Latest news Get a Demo Close Trigger Solution DatuBIM Progress Tracking Stakeholders Datumate for owners Datumate for General Contractors Datumate for Engineering & Consulting (E&C) firms Use Cases Resources Blog Case Studies Webinars FAQs Glossary Company About Us News and events Careers Partners Contact us Get a Demo Press Releases Introducing DatuBIM Progress Tracking: Percent Complete You Can Defend September 1, 2026 Datumate has released DatuBIM Progress Tracking , a new module that turns percent complete from a judgment call into a measurement. It links a project’s Primavera P6 or Microsoft Project schedule to its design geometry and to the drone data heavy civil teams already capture — producing a weighted completion figure and a forecast end date with an audit trail behind them. Progress Tracking is generally available to DatuBIM customers as of September 1, 2026. Percent complete is the most expensive guess on your project On most heavy civil jobs, percent complete is produced by a person. A superintendent walks the site, forms a judgment, and enters a number into the schedule. That number moves the pay application. It moves resourcing. It moves the date committed to the owner. And there is rarely an artifact behind it that anyone can point to. Three things break on nearly every project: By the time the schedule updates, it’s history. Site conditions change weekly. Schedules update monthly, if that. Design, schedule, and site data don’t talk. Design lives in CAD or IFC. The schedule lives in P6 or MS Project. Reality lives in drone flights and photos. The three get reconciled by hand, if at all. The forecast is a feeling. Everyone on the job knows what’s slipping. Nobody can say by how many days. The knowledge is real — it just sits in three systems and one person’s head, and none of it adds up to a number anyone can defend in the owner’s meeting. One model, three anchors Progress Tracking closes a gap the industry has bridged manually for two decades. Every tracked activity is anchored in three places at once: Anchored to your schedule. P6 and MS Project import with activity IDs and hierarchy preserved. Anchored to your design. 2D CAD and IFC geometry becomes named, measurable objects. Anchored to reality. Your own site capture, recorded object by object. How DatuBIM Progress Tracking works 1. Import the schedule you already have Users upload a Microsoft Project or Primavera P6 file to a Gantt viewer, where they can search for activities, filter for those with geometric units, isolate the critical path, and change the time scale. Activity IDs and hierarchy are preserved, so planners keep working in their own tools. Teams without a schedule in the system can build standalone activities instead. 2. Turn the design into measurable objects The Design Object Editor converts CAD geometry into named, manageable objects — by selecting entities directly, sweeping a polygon or rectangle around an area, or letting DatuBIM detect repeated blocks and consistent layers for confirmation. Object types a designer never defined can be created by the user. Critically, this works from 2D CAD, not only from a 3D BIM model. 3. Link objects to activities Once objects are tied to schedule activities, planned dates populate automatically from the Gantt, and actual start, actual end, inspection status, and approval status are recorded in the same panel. Four disconnected records become one. 4. Record what is actually built Activities can be measured by count, length, area, volume, mass or straight percentage — matching the units projects are billed in. Every progress entry carries its own date, which can be adjusted so a late update lands on the day the work actually happened. Field crews update the same activities from the DatuBIM Onsite mobile app, attaching photos, voice notes, video and documents as evidence on the activity itself. Weighted, not averaged Completion rolls up into a single dashboard, weighted by the contribution of each activity. Backfilling and drilling piles are not the same amount of project — they differ in cost, resources, duration, technical complexity, and critical-path impact — and counting them equally produces a percentage that means nothing.
